claims.text: Conventionally processed nuclear-grade stainless steel has a largely random grain-boundary character distribution.
Conventionally processed nuclear-grade stainless steel forms a heterogeneous passive film.
The controlled study will compare cyclically deformed and annealed samples with untreated controls.
Cyclic deformation followed by short-duration recrystallization annealing near 800 °C will refine the grain-boundary network and increase the fraction of low-energy or special boundaries.
Increasing the fraction of low-energy or special grain boundaries promotes formation of a more uniform and chemically robust passive oxide film.
The engineered grain-boundary network lowers overall grain-boundary energy.
Deformation followed by recrystallization annealing lowers microstructural defect or dislocation density.
Lower grain-boundary energy and defect density facilitate rapid and spatially uniform passive-film formation.
A uniform passive film with low defect density mitigates localized pitting.
Improved passive-film quality increases the corrosion resistance of the engineered steel.
Engineered samples will exhibit greater passive-film thickness uniformity, greater chemical homogeneity, and lower film defect density than untreated samples.
Engineered samples will exhibit higher pitting breakdown potentials than untreated samples.
Engineered samples will exhibit lower corrosion current densities than untreated samples.
The controlled tests will use 3.5% NaCl aqueous solution at room temperature and identical electrochemical exposure for treated and untreated samples.
Cyclic anodic exposure in room-temperature 3.5% NaCl simulates service conditions in chemical-processing pipelines and nuclear-power applications.

The proposed mechanism should hold under moderate-temperature, chloride-rich aqueous conditions but may fail at extreme temperatures or in highly aggressive chemical environments where other corrosion mechanisms dominate.
Variations in alloy composition can alter passivation and corrosion resistance.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in both passive-film properties and electrochemical corrosion metrics relative to untreated controls would falsify the hypothesis.
